newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian reaches contract with attendants.
newsitem.headline: Canadian reaches contract with attendants.

text.p: Canadian Airlines International Ltd reached a tentative contract with the union representing its 2,700 flight attendants, opening the door to talks with the rest of its unions on a corporate survival plan.

Canadian Airlines, Canada's second largest but troubled national airline, said on Sunday it reached an accord late Saturday with the Canadian Union of Public Employees on a 38-month collective agreement with the flight attendants. They had been without a contract for a year.

The contract, subject to ratification by the membership, puts the union at par with Canadian's five other unions in achieving improved productivity, the company said. Terms of the new agreement were not to be disclosed until after ratification.

As part of the agreement the union's bargaining team agreed to join discussions already under way in Richmond, British Columbia, with the other unions on the company's restructuring plan, which includes a 10 percent pay cut for all employees.
The money-losing airline has said its proposed 1997 business plan is aimed at saving some $180 million a year.

"I am delighted we now have a tentative agreement with our flight attendants, and that their union, CUPE, is joining the other unions to get an agreement on the 1997 business plan," Canadian president Kevin Benson said in a statement.
Canadian's six unions, representing 16,400 employees, had refused to enter the restructuring talks with the airline until the flight attendants had a new contract.
Canadian has set a November 30 deadline to put together a restructuring which they said was necessary for the survival of the airline.

The powerful Canadian Auto Workers Union representing 3,700 terminal staff, however, has rejected the 10 percent pay cut proposal and has asked the federal government to help out, including re-regulating the airline industry.

Federal Transportation Minister David Anderson said Ottawa would consider some kind of aid if Canadian reaches an agreement with its employees but warned the government would not consider re-regulating the industry.
